narrative:
This was a textbook, fully automated recon chain run by the student against their own box (192.168.92.131) from 192.168.92.129, lasting under 15 minutes end-to-end. It began quietly: a slow trickle of single SYN probes to port 80 starting at 09:51Z (firewall.log), followed by an apparent robots.txt pull via curl. Then at 10:03:19Z the real nmap scan fired -sV -sC against the top 1000 ports, producing the dense, multi-TTL SYN burst visible in firewall.log across dozens of ports (22, 443, 3389, 8080, etc.) within a five-second window -- the classic signature of a scripted scanner forging packet TTLs/IDs. sshd logged OpenSSL version-mismatch noise as a side effect of the port-22 probes, not real auth attempts.

Once port 80 was confirmed, the tool chain pivoted to HTTP: WhatWeb fingerprinting (not distinctly visible in the logs), an Nmap NSE HTTP probe (GET / and PROPFIND /, clearly tagged with the Nmap Scripting Engine user-agent), then content discovery via gobuster and ffuf. These brute-forced common.txt and a generated wordlist against /, /admin/, and /backup/, producing over 14,000 requests and a flood of 404s -- but critically surfacing two real HTTP 200 hits: /admin/ and /backup/index.html, both confirmed independently by the recon agent's own fetch_page calls.

From the defender's side, the hunt record reconstructed almost the entire chain purely from firewall SYN logs and access.log user-agent strings, even though a few individual fetch_page steps (backup/, admin/index.html, generate_wordlist, and two placeholder ffuf calls) left no distinguishable trace in the evidence provided. No evidence of actual authentication or exploitation exists in ssh.log -- this was reconnaissance only, stopping right at the edge of exploitation.

steps.note: The nmap -sV -sC run generated the bulk SYN sweep against ~1000 ports (varying TTLs/source ports consistent with nmap's raw packet crafting) seen in firewall.log from 10:03:20-10:03:25Z. This specific entry matches a probe timed one second after the nmap start (10:03:19Z UTC). Its HTTP NSE scripts also produced GET / and PROPFIND / requests at 10:03:31Z (see log_lines entry '5: 192.168.92.129 - - [27/Oct/2026:10:03:31 +0000] "PROPFIND / HTTP/1.1" 405 564 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nmap Scripting Engine; https://nmap.org/book/nse.html)"').
steps.detection: IDS/firewall alert on a single source IP generating a high-volume, short-interval SYN burst to dozens/hundreds of distinct destination ports (port-scan threshold rule); web server WAF/IDS signature for Nmap NSE User-Agent and PROPFIND method on non-WebDAV server.

steps.note: whatweb's HTTP fingerprinting GET to port 80 would produce a generic access.log GET / entry, but no distinct WhatWeb user-agent string appears anywhere in the supplied log_lines (only curl and Nmap NSE user-agents are present around this time), so this specific request was not captured in the evidence given.
steps.detection: Web server access log review for the WhatWeb default user-agent string (e.g. 'WhatWeb/x.x'); correlate low-volume single-GET bursts immediately following a completed port scan.

steps.note: A GET /robots.txt from 192.168.92.129 appears in access.log, though logged with a curl/8.21.0 user-agent and at 09:55:24Z rather than the recon tool's claimed 'ai-recon-agent (study tool)' UA and 10:03:46Z timestamp -- indicating either a clock offset or an earlier unrelated probe reusing the same path. It is the only robots.txt fetch tied to this attacker IP in the evidence.
steps.detection: Log monitoring for requests to robots.txt (low severity but a common recon marker) correlated with other recon indicators from the same source IP in a short window.

steps.note: No GET /backup/ (plain, pre-gobuster) line for 192.168.92.129 appears anywhere in the supplied access.log excerpts; the log_lines are capped at 300 and dominated by the later gobuster/ffuf 404 flood, so this single fetch_page request is not present in the evidence provided.
steps.detection: Access log alerting on first-time access to non-standard, sensitive-sounding directories like /backup/ from an external/scanning IP.

steps.note: The gobuster run against the web root (started 10:03:49Z) is directly evidenced by its distinct user-agent string 'gobuster/3.8.2' appearing in access.log, including the 200 hit on /admin/ discovered during this sweep.
steps.detection: WAF/IDS signature for gobuster User-Agent string; rate-based alert on very high request-rate / high-404-rate from a single IP within seconds (brute-force directory enumeration pattern).

steps.note: This fetch_page GET /admin/ at 10:03:57Z is directly matched by an access.log line with the exact timestamp and the recon agent's own user-agent string 'ai-recon-agent (study tool)', distinct from the later gobuster hit on the same path two seconds later.
steps.detection: Access log alert on any 200 response from a brute-force/recon tool user-agent hitting a sensitive directory path such as /admin/.

steps.note: The second gobuster invocation targeting /backup wordlist is reflected in the large set of /backup/* 404 probe lines (e.g. /backup/admin, /backup/phpmyadmin, /backup/wp-login) attributed to 192.168.92.129, consistent with gobuster's common.txt wordlist appended to the /backup/ base path, run 10:03:57-10:03:59Z.
steps.detection: Rate/volume alert for repeated 404 responses under a single subdirectory path from one source IP within a few seconds (directory brute-force signature).

steps.note: The third gobuster invocation targeting /admin wordlist matches the large set of /admin/* 404 and 403 probe lines (e.g. /admin/.bash_history, /admin/.ssh, /admin/.htaccess [403]) attributed to 192.168.92.129, consistent with gobuster/common.txt enumeration under /admin/, run 10:03:59-10:04:00Z.
steps.detection: Same directory-bruteforce rate alert as step 7, scoped to /admin/ path; WAF rule blocking repeated requests for sensitive dotfiles (.bash_history, .ssh, .htaccess).

steps.note: generate_wordlist is a local, offline recon-agent operation (building a custom FUZZ wordlist file on the attacker's own machine) that makes no network request to the target, so it cannot appear in the target's firewall/access/ssh logs by design.
steps.detection: Not detectable from target-side logs; only visible via attacker-host forensics/process monitoring (e.g., file creation audit on the recon host).

steps.note: This ffuf invocation record has command 'n/a' and no target/URL specified, suggesting it was a dry-run, config-only, or failed-to-launch step; no corresponding ffuf traffic distinguishable from this specific call appears in access.log.
steps.detection: Access log monitoring for ffuf User-Agent ('Fuzz Faster U Fool') and the -e extension-based request bursts; this step produced no identifiable network evidence to alert on.

steps.note: Identical to step 10 - command 'n/a', likely a preparatory/placeholder ffuf call before the fully-specified invocations in steps 12-13; no distinguishable log evidence.
steps.detection: Same as step 10 - would need request-level correlation by exact timestamp/URL which is not available for this placeholder entry.

steps.note: The ffuf run against /admin/FUZZ with extensions .php/.txt/.zip/.sql/.bak is reflected by the 'Fuzz Faster U Fool v2.1.0-dev' user-agent appearing in the access.log summary alongside admin-path probe entries (e.g., /admin/84fa926a-... random UUID canary request typical of ffuf calibration), run 10:04:20-10:04:25Z.
steps.detection: WAF/IDS signature for ffuf User-Agent string ('Fuzz Faster U Fool'); alert on burst of requests with multiple file-extension permutations against a single path in a short window.

steps.note: The parallel ffuf run against /backup/FUZZ with the same extension list is reflected by the same 'Fuzz Faster U Fool v2.1.0-dev' user-agent tag covering /backup/* probe entries, run 10:04:25Z (very short duration, consistent with an early hit/cutoff or small response set).
steps.detection: Same ffuf UA/burst-rate detection as step 12, applied to the /backup/ path; also monitor for ffuf's extension-permutation pattern (-e .php,.txt,.zip,.sql,.bak) against directory roots.

steps.note: No access.log line for a specific GET /admin/index.html request attributed to 192.168.92.129 appears anywhere in the provided evidence; the log excerpt around 10:04:38Z only shows the /backup/index.html 200 hit, so this companion request to /admin/index.html (likely 404, no index.html under /admin/) is not present in the given evidence.
steps.detection: Full access log retention/search for GET requests to /admin/index.html from the recon IP, cross-referenced by exact timestamp with the fetch_page tool call at 10:04:38Z.

steps.note: Direct exact match: the fetch_page call for /backup/index.html at 10:04:38Z corresponds precisely in time, path, and user-agent ('ai-recon-agent (study tool)') to this access.log line, confirming the agent's own direct verification request after ffuf/gobuster found the directory.
steps.detection: Access log alert on 200 response for backup/index-type files combined with recon-tool user-agent strings; data-loss-prevention check on whether backup/index.html exposes sensitive content.

detection_ideas.idea: Deploy a network IDS (Suricata/Snort) rule alerting on a single source IP sending SYN packets to >20 distinct destination ports within 60 seconds -- classic port-scan signature that would have caught the nmap sweep immediately at 10:03:20-25Z (and the earlier slow probe at 09:51-09:55Z).
detection_ideas.mitre: T1595.001 - Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks

detection_ideas.idea: Add WAF/reverse-proxy User-Agent blocklist/alerting for known recon tool signatures: 'Nmap Scripting Engine', 'gobuster', 'Fuzz Faster U Fool (ffuf)', and generic tool UAs; auto-block or CAPTCHA-challenge after N matches from one IP.

Set a rate-based alert/block for any single source IP generating a high 404-response ratio (e.g., >50 requests/min with >90% 404) against the web root -- would have caught the 14,558-request gobuster/ffuf directory brute force quickly instead of after the fact.
detection_ideas.data_source: access.log aggregate/rate analysis (e.g., fail2ban, WAF rate limiting)

detection_ideas.idea: Restrict or authenticate access to /admin/ and /backup/ at the application layer (IP allowlist, basic auth, or remove from public web root) since both returned HTTP 200 and were discoverable -- the single most actionable finding of this engagement.

Centralize and time-synchronize all host logs (firewall, web, auth) to NTP/UTC and forward to a SIEM so that correlation across tools does not depend on manually reconciling clock offsets between attacker and target systems.
detection_ideas.data_source: SIEM / log aggregation pipeline, NTP configuration
detection_ideas.mitre: T1070 - Indicator Removal (supports overall detection engineering / log integrity)
